newsitem.title: TURKEY: Moslem nations plan summit meeting in Turkey.
newsitem.headline: Moslem nations plan summit meeting in Turkey.

text.p: Turkey's Islamist Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan on Saturday hosted a meeting of ministers from eight Moslem countries in Istanbul aimed at boosting economic cooperation among them.
Ministers from Turkey, Egypt, Iran, Pakistan, Nigeria, Bangladesh, Malaysia and Indonesia gathered in the city to plan a summit between their leaders in the first quarter of this year, Erbakan said.
"Our aim is for this meeting to be profitable not just for these countries, but for all humanity," Erbakan said in a speech at the start of the one-day talks.

Erbakan has visited all the participating countries, except Bangladesh, since coming to power in June. During that time he has given priority to strengthening secular, but Moslem, Turkey's links with the Islamic world.
These moves have been a source of friction between Erbakan and NATO-member Turkey's western allies, notably the United States.
In December, Iranian President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani made a visit to Turkey which drew criticism from the United States which has tried to isolate Tehran internationally.
Washington was also annoyed by a $23 billion agreement which Turkey signed in August for the supply of Iranian natural gas over 23 years.

Preparatory work on the organisation, known as D-8 (Developing-Eight) and to be based in Istanbul, began last year following Erbakan's foreign trips. Officials previously met in November to discuss the group's development.

Erbakan said the areas of cooperation would include banking, tourism, energy, transport, the environment, privatisation and research. He said the grouping would also seek to boost cooperation with non-Moslem countries.

Political analysts say Erbakan's efforts coincide with a straining in relations between Turkey and the European Union. EU aid to Turkey has been suspended over concern about Ankara's human rights record and after opposition from member Greece.
"This could be described as Turkey's attempt to form a 'local league' in which it will feel more comfortable than in the European league," the liberal daily Yeni Yuzyil said in an editorial.
But Turkish officials say the grouping will not block member nations from fulfilling their obligations to other international organisations.
Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller told delegates at the meeting that D-8 marked a further development of Turkey's international relations, extending beyond existing links with Europe.
Ankara is already a member of the Economic Cooperation Organisation, formed with Iran and Pakistan and since expanded to include former Soviet Central Asian republics.
The foreign ministers of Iran and Pakistan will also hold a trilateral meeting with Turkish officials on Sunday to discuss the situation in Afghanistan.
An international conference aimed at halting the fighting in Afghanistan was held in Tehran in October. Pakistan, a key player in the region, stayed away from that meeting.
